summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed.

The Interior Ministry's statistics service records that anti-LGBT+ offences concentrate in urban units of more than 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris. The Paris rate of 22 recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants is roughly three times the national figure of 7.

Paris Pride, held on 28 June 2025, was classified a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry. National police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with officers positioned to separate opposing groups.

Paris holds the country's densest LGBT commercial and social infrastructure and its only officially organised gaybourhoods, and hosts the annual Marche des Fiertés. A 2004 count recorded 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops in the city.
tangentialFactors:
The statistics service attributes part of Paris's elevated rate to victims who are not residents of the city and to commuters, so the figure reflects the capital's role as a regional destination and workplace rather than a uniform residential risk.

Targeted violence against LGBT public figures in the region has a documented history. Bertrand Delanoë, elected Paris's first openly gay mayor in 2002, was stabbed that year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals.
localsOnly:
The region's LGBT venues, organisations and the annual Marche des Fiertés are concentrated in Paris; residents of the outer parts of the region travel into the capital for comparable infrastructure.

Recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in the region are concentrated in urban units above 200,000 inhabitants, which covers the capital and the surrounding built-up area where most residents live.
outOfScopeNotes:
The statistics service compiles anti-LGBT+ offences as a single category and does not disaggregate them by trans status, so trans-specific incidence in the region is not sourced.

The 140-venue count for Paris dates from 2004; no current figure for the region's LGBT infrastructure is available.

Whether the 2025 Paris Pride passed without incident under the reinforced police presence is not documented.
